title: Ecclesiastes 4:9–16
context: Ecclesiastes 4:9–16 begins with the sayings about companionship: two are better than one, because they can help, warm, and defend one another, and “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (4:12). The saying recalls the creation word “It is not good for the man to be alone.” (Genesis 2:18). Christian readers have often applied the threefold cord to marriage or friendship with God at the center, an application that goes beyond the verse’s plain sense but is not foreign to the book’s concern for companionship. The section then tells of a poor and wise youth who is better than an old and foolish king who no longer receives admonition, and of crowds who follow a successor yet will not rejoice in him later (4:13–16). The identities of the king and the youth are not given, and the Hebrew of 4:14–16 can be read in more than one way, for example whether one youth or two are in view; this draft does not identify them or settle the details. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground: human companionship is a gift, and political popularity, like other achievements under the sun, does not last.

verses.text: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.
verses.arminianNotes:
Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. Companionship is commended.

Arminian readers see the verse as encouragement to build relationships of mutual help, and they note that people are responsible to seek and maintain such partnerships rather than to labor in isolation like the man of 4:8.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the saying echoes the creation word that it is not good for the man to be alone (Genesis 2:18), and they see companionship as part of the good order God built into human life.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the value of companionship in work and life, and both apply it broadly to friendship and community.

verses.text: For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.
verses.arminianNotes:
If they fall, one will lift up his fellow, but woe to him who is alone when he falls with no one to lift him. The image is practical.

Arminian readers note that mutual help is a real choice of love, and they see the verse as encouraging believers to care for one another in times of failure and weakness, a theme that applies to the life of faith as well as daily life.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the verse as describing the help God often provides through others, and they note that the New Testament calls believers to restore one another gently (compare Galatians 6:1–2).

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about mutual care and the danger of isolation.

verses.text: Again, if two lie together, then they have warmth; but how can one keep warm alone?
verses.arminianNotes:
If two lie together, they have warmth, but how can one keep warm alone? The example comes from ordinary life, perhaps travelers on a cold night.

Arminian readers see a simple picture of comfort shared, and they note that wisdom literature often teaches through ordinary images that every reader can recognize from experience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the verse need not be limited to marriage, though it can include it, and they see in it the general good of companionship that God provides for human beings in a harsh world.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and avoid narrowing it to a single application, holding open the setting the Preacher may have in mind.

verses.text: If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
verses.arminianNotes:
If someone prevails against one who is alone, two can withstand him, and “a threefold cord is not quickly broken.” The sayings build from two to three.

Arminian readers note the strength of shared commitment, and they see the threefold cord as an image of relationships strengthened by mutual faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Christian readers have often applied the threefold cord to marriage or friendship with God at the center, while recognizing that the verse itself makes a general point about strength in numbers.

Both traditions treat that application as a later reading that goes beyond the plain sense, and they read the verse as shared ground about the strength of companionship.

verses.text: Better is a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who doesn’t know how to receive admonition any more.
verses.arminianNotes:
Better is a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knows how to receive admonition. Wisdom outranks position.

Arminian readers note that the king’s refusal to receive correction is a choice that has made him foolish, and they see the verse as a warning that age and status do not protect anyone from the consequences of rejecting counsel.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the verse reverses ordinary expectations, valuing a teachable heart over power and experience, and they see the theme of God exalting the humble elsewhere in Scripture (compare 1 Samuel 2:7–8).

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the value of teachability and do not identify the king or the youth.

verses.text: For out of prison he came out to be king; yes, even in his kingdom he was born poor.
verses.arminianNotes:
For out of prison he came out to be king; yes, even in his kingdom he was born poor. The verse is ambiguous about who is meant.

Arminian readers note that the text may refer to the youth rising from prison or poverty, or to the king, and they read it as an illustration of how fortunes reverse rather than as a reference to a known person.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note that some interpreters have proposed historical figures such as Joseph, but the text does not name anyone, and they hold such suggestions loosely.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the reversals of fortune under the sun and avoid settling the identity of the person described.

verses.text: I saw all the living who walk under the sun, that they were with the youth, the other, who succeeded him.
verses.arminianNotes:
He sees all the living who walk under the sun with the youth, the other, who succeeded him. The crowd follows the new ruler.

Arminian readers note the fickleness of popular support, and they see the verse as a warning against placing ultimate hope in leaders, however promising they may appear at the beginning.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the phrase the other, who succeeded him may introduce a second youth, and they hold the reading open, since the Hebrew of 4:14–16 can be taken in more than one way.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the passing nature of political popularity and do not resolve the uncertain details.

verses.text: There was no end of all the people, even of all them over whom he was—yet those who come after shall not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and a chasing after wind.
verses.arminianNotes:
There is no end of the people he ruled, yet those who come after will not rejoice in him; this also is vanity and a chasing after wind. Popularity fades.

Arminian readers note that even widely supported leaders are soon forgotten, and they see the verse as calling people to seek a lasting good beyond reputation and success.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the conclusion matches the book’s theme that human achievements do not last under the sun (compare 2:16), and they see it as directing hope toward God, whose works endure forever (3:14).

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the transience of human fame and the futility of resting one’s hope on it.
